description.narrative: The development objective of Disaster Risk Management Development Policy Loan with a Catastrophe-Deferred Drawdown Option (CAT DDO) Project is to strengthen Serbia's institutional and legal framework to effectively manage the physical and fiscal impact of natural hazards. This objective will be achieved by supporting policy reforms under three operational pillars: (i) Strengthening the Borrower's legal and institutional framework for post-disaster reconstruction and disaster and climate risk management; (ii) Strengthening the Borrower's technical capacity for planning and implementing disaster and climate risk management activities; (iii) Reducing the fiscal impact and strengthening the Borrower's financial capacity to respond to the adverse impact of natural hazards, particularly those exacerbated by climate change. This operation is a key component in the efforts of the government to shift to a more comprehensive cross-sectoral approach for Disaster Risk Management (DRM). The World Bank has been supporting the development of Serbia's catastrophe insurance market through the South East Europe and Caucasus Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (SEEC CRIF) since 2011. The CAT-DDO will provide the Government with a fiscal buffer to reduce the impact of future disasters on its fiscal balance as well as critical bridge financing for immediate response.
The objective is to strengthen Serbia's institutional and legal framework to effectively manage the physical and fiscal impact of natural hazards.

title.narrative: B2-Number of sectors and institutions that are using an open-source geospatial platform with risk information.

comment.narrative:
<p><strong><em><em>Result Indicator B2 has been significantly exceeded</em>.</em></strong> GeoSerbia – a national Spatial Data Infrastructure (SDI) – which allows for improved access to Serbia’s spatial data (electronic geographic data) has beendeveloped. This platform provides critical information for risk assessment and risk-informed decision-making at the national and local levels. The Law on National Infrastructure of Geospatial Data (Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia No. 27/2018, April 6, 2018) provides the legal framework for the national SDI. As an open-source geospatial platform, it is available for public viewing and full data access can be requested by state institutions. There are 146 institutions which are registered as active users of the platform, including 25 ministries/government agencies, 107 municipalities and cities, 4 are bodies of the autonomous province and 9 public enterprises and companies. These institutions span an array of sectors like environment, agriculture, real-estate, urban planning, geology, water, and transport. At the end of July 2020, the cumulative number of users of the national geoportal was 1,033,010, while the cumulative number of queries on geodata via the national geoportal was 33,480,398. In addition, the Geodetic Authority of Serbia (RGA) also leverages the GeoSerbia platform to assist various Ministries in creating analytics as a basis for designingand planning a wide range of investments and activities. For example, the RGA has been using the GeoSerbia platform in collaboration with the Ministry of Culture to identify culture heritage and archaeological sites and assess risks related to disasters. Additionally, the PIMO developed the Disaster Risk Information System (DRIS) on this platform as part of the larger Disaster Risk Registry platform that is currently being created (in collaboration with the RGA) to consolidate a centralized repository of risk information at the national level. Efforts are currently ongoing to establish a formally link data on GeoSerbia and DRIS. The availability of risk data on GeoSerbia enabled municipalities and local government to develop rescue plans and disaster risk reduction investment plans based on quantified risk information. Result B2 thus helped strengthen the institutional framework for better managing both physical and fiscal risks through enhanced technical capacity, coordination and awareness of contingent liabilities for planning and implementing risk management activities. <em>???????Sources: ISR, October 2020; ICR interviews, February 2021</em></p>
<p> </p>

title.narrative: B3-Number of sectors and local self-governments that have applied the post-disaster loss and needs assessment methodology.

comment.narrative: <p><strong><em>Result Indicator B3 has been achieved.</em></strong> In a flood event in June 2019, 23 local governments were affected. Of the affected LSGs, 19 or 82 percent of LSGs affected applied the PDNA methodology to assess damages and losses of this event and subsequent recovery programs developed were based on the data collected and provided by the affected municipalities. The PDNAs developed covered the five sectors of housing, agriculture, public facilities, economy, and infrastructure and thus also achieved the target of 3 sectors<em>. </em>???????During project execution, various PDNA training events were also organized, covering an estimated 70 local self-governments, and resulting in a high uptake of a post disaster needs assessment. Most local governments have continued to apply the methodology to assess the damages and losses in the aftermath of disasters despite the PDNA methodology not being mandatory by law indicating local interest and benefits. Currently a needs assessment methodology exists at the national level which is similar to the PDNA methodology but is considered as outdated in term of reflecting current institutional structures. The GoS through the PIMO is at the moment undertaking efforts to update the national methodology and align it with the PDNA. It should be noted that ISR documents considered the target as the percentage of all LSGs in Serbia that employed the PDNA and not just the percntage of those affected by disaster events. However, the indicator when evaluated on the basis of LSGs affected by disaster events and not on the basis of the total number of LSGs in Serbia, provides for a more valid reflection of the associated prior action and is better aligned with the PDO. <em>Sources: ISR October 2020; ICR interviews, February 2021; Local PDNA reports and summary of PDNA for 2019 floods report. </em></p>

title.narrative: C3-A report on consolidated information on historical post-disaster expenditure data is produced annually and submitted to the Budget Department.

baseline.value: Consolidated historical post-disaster expenditure information not collected.

target.value: Data collected and submitted to the Budget Department.

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Indicator C3 has been achieved in December 2020. </strong>???????The Bank provided support for the collection and consolidation of the post-disaster expenditure data. The Fiscal risk sector collected data from almost 30 State- owned enterprises on disaster related expenditures and received associated data the Treasury. The data was consolidated, and the post-disaster expenditure database was delivered at the end of 2020. The data will support national budget planning, helping with more efficient management of fiscal impacts from natural hazards (i.e., based on quantified information). <em>???????Source: ICR interviews, February 2021; Note of Disaster Risk Financing dataset; Central Government Budget expenditure file</em></p>

actual.value: Consolidated historical post disaster expenditure data collected and submitted to the Budget Department

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result Indicator B1 has been achieved. </strong>A National Flood Risk Assessment covering all 75 flood prone areas in the country has been completed .The final report and map/risk atlas were completed by the end of October 2020, and with this Serbia reached the end of the first risk assessment cycle under the EU Flood Directive. To guide this assessment, and fully in line with the EU Flood Directive, the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Water Management adopted a national flood risk asessment methodology in the form of a “Rulebook on Establishing Methodology for Development of Flood Vulnerability and Flood Risk Maps.” The assessment of these 75 flood prone areas covered a total length of 2,750 km of river reaches. The flood risk assessment against a 100-year return period identified that 115 towns and municipalities (having a population of 5.5 million – approximately 75 percent of the total population of Serbia) are exposed to potential flooding. The comprehensive assessment was regarded as a fundamental step towards strengthening Serbia’s capacity, among other things, for risk mitigation works, such as dikes or retention areas, restricting building in high-risk flood zones, and improving hydro meteorological forecasting. <em>Sources: Final report "Flood Hazard and Risk Mapping: Component 2 of Serbia National Disaster Risk Management Plan (NDRMP)"; ISR October 2020; ICR interviews, February 2021</em>???????</p>

title.narrative: C2-GoS prepared and enacted a set of fiscal incentives and a model DRFI plan for local governments to facilitate wider use of budgetary protection instruments against the financial consequences of nat

target.value: Fiscal incentives enacted and at least 3 municipalities have adopted a DRF plan including the information and capacity to access disaster risk insurance.

comment.narrative:
<p><strong><em>Indicator C2 has been partially achieved. </em></strong>Three pilot municipalities - Ucize, Paracin and Kraljevo – have prepared disaster risk financing plans. This built on previous work supported by the World Bank TA program on assessing the legal framework for Disaster risk financing (DRF) at the municipal level, analyzing past disaster related expenditures, and training local self-government on DRF. However, the indicator is assessed as partially achieved, since the adoption of these plans experienced delays – in part, due to constraints imposed at the LSGs by the continuing COVID-19 pandemic but more so because LSGs didnot consider adoption of DRF plans as their priority task, since such plans were not mandated by law. Even though the fiscal incentives to use risk transfer solutions as originally envisaged under this indicator are yet to be enacted, to accelerate efforts on this front and motivate LSGs to rely less on public funding and leverage risk financing solutions, the GoS has embedded DRF plans as a component in the local disaster risk reduction plans— which local governments are mandated to develop and adopt. Notwithstanding the constraints imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic, so far five DRR plans that incorporate DRF have been developed and their adoption is expected in the coming months. In parallel, the Government has made provisions for facilitating trainings on the development of DRRs which would include a DRF component. It is likely, based on the ongoing efforts of the Government that in 2022, more local governments would have considered and adopted DRF in their planning processes. <em>???????Source: ICR interviews, February 2021; Local DRF plans</em></p>
<p> </p>

actual.value: 3 Local governments have developed DRF plans. Formal adoption at the time of ICR preparation has not occurred but is likely in 2022.

title.narrative: C1-Fiscal risk unit established, staffed, and functioning as demonstrated by (a) adoption of the Systematization Act which sets out the number of positions and (b) the identification and quantificatio

target.value: Staffed, contingent liabilities from disasters identified and quantified, and fiscal risk statement published.

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Indicator C1 has been achieved in January 2021</strong>. Fiscal Risk Unit was systematized as a separate group within the Macroeconomic and Fiscal Analyses and Projections Department (MFAD) of the Ministry of Finance through the Systematization Act adopted on 16 March 2018 by the Government (Conclusion No. 110-2322/2018) with the responsibility for fiscal risk management. The group has since been elevated to a sector. Staffing of the Fiscal Risk Sector is growing and currently stands at fourteen eople, including a head of sector. Since the establishment of the unit, the Bank has provided TA for the quantification of disaster related contingent liabilities. The Bank, through a SECO financed TA, also supported the production of a fiscal risk statement which was achieved the end of 2020. <em>Source</em>: <em>ICR interviews, February 2021; ISR October 2020</em></p>

actual.value: Fiscal risk unit staffed and contingent liabilities from disasters identified and quantified, and fiscal risk statement published.

title.narrative: A1- PIMO staffed and functioning as demonstrated by the adoption of a Systematization Act and submission of Annual Reports to the Borrower's Cabinet

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator A1 has been achieved. ???????</strong>In September 2017, the Government of Serbia adopted a System atization Act for the PIMO, which set out its responsibilities and number of staff positions, contributing to strengthen the legal and institutional framework to manage physical and fiscal impacts from natural hazards. The PIMO prepared and submitted the 2017, 2018, and 2019 annual reports to the Cabinet for approval. All these reports were formally adopted by the Government. The  reports covered the required post-disaster data and information, enabling better planning based on quantified information. The PIMO is currently staffed with 73 employees across engineering, coordination, legal, financial, logistical, and technical services. PIMO is currently managing various reconstruction and recovery projects financed by different development partners, including the World Bank, the European Investment Bank (EIB), the Council of Europe Development Bank (CEB), and the KfW Development Bank. <em>Sources: Mission aide memoires 2017-2020; ISR, October 2020; ICR interviews conducted in February 2021???????</em></p>

actual.value: The PIMO is staffed and annual reports submitted

title.narrative: A2-Systematization Act to operationalize a new government institution or agency to implement Law on Natural and other Hazard Risk Reduction and Emergency Management adopted.

target.value: Borrower has adopted a Systematization Act.

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Result indicator A2 has been achieved.</strong> The Law on Disaster Risk Reduction and Emergency Management was adopted by the National Assembly in November 2018 (published in the National Gazette of the Republic of Serbia NO.87/2018, dated 21 November 2018) and the Systematization Act for the Ministry of Interior formalized the role of the Sector for Emergency Management (SEM) as the lead entity for implementing this Law. The Law mandates, inter alia, that risk assessments are conducted at the ntional and local level, including the development of the respective local protection and rescue plans. Before this Law came into force SEM’s responsibility was limited to response, protection and rescue in case of disasters. The Law introduced additional responsibilities to SEM, such as overseeing all risk assessment and monitoring activities, including risk reduction planning and the respective implementation of risk reduction measures by all administrative units from local to national, government sector institutions, and large public and commercial enterprises. As a result of these reforms, SEM supervised the completion of the National Flood Risk Assessment. Such risk assessments enabled the development of rescue plans and disaster risk reduction (DRR) investment plans by local governments. Out of 174 Serbian local self-governments, 132 received the approval from the Ministry of Interior for their Local Disaster Risk Assessments, of which 65 subsequently received approval for the development of Protection and Rescue Plans. The development of risk assessments and rescue plans not only enabled risk reduction planning but, in the process, also reduced contingent liabilities. <em>???????Sources: Mission aide memoires 2018-2020; ISR October 2020; ICR interviews conducted in February 2021</em>???????</p>

actual.value: The Borrower has adopted a systemization act formalizing the Sector for Emergency Management (SEM) as the lead entity for implementing the law
